name: Arikara

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A shared government and distinct peoples
claimBlocks.text: MHA Nation’s official site identifies the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation at Fort Berthold in North Dakota. It describes a Tribal Business Council with a chairman and representatives from six segments. This provides institutional orientation to a shared government; it does not make Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara interchangeable names or turn the reservation into their entire historical homeland.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Homepage Mission, Tribal Government and Our Land

claimBlocks.text: MHA Nation’s history distinguishes Sahnish village movements from Mandan and Hidatsa histories. Its narrative and timeline differ between 1862 and 1863, so the move into Like-a-Fishhook is described here as the early 1860s. The page also recounts Garrison Dam relocation as a loss of fertile bottomlands and connected communities, with relocation completed by fall 1954.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Arikara section; Village & Relocations; Elbowoods & Garrison Dam Relocations; Fort Berthold Indian Reservation

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Language priorities and community educational work
claimBlocks.text: MHA Nation presents Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara as separate languages and acknowledges Elders, teachers, Nueta Hidatsa Sahnish College and the MHA Language Project. Its portal identifies learning materials and past Arikara class recordings. This is an institutional account of educational priorities and collaboration; listing resources does not establish their contents, effectiveness or present class schedules as independently checked.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Language introduction; Recognizing Our Community’s Language Work; Learning Resources; Arikara class-recording notice

claimBlocks.text: North Dakota Studies identifies Sahnish as the people’s own name and places Arikara village history along the Missouri River. Its educational account describes earthlodge homes, gardening of corn, beans and squash, food preservation and hunting. It also discusses epidemics and movement toward Like-a-Fishhook. These selected historical explanations do not describe every family or establish present practices.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Naming paragraph; selected village/home/gardening paragraphs; epidemic/movement account and conclusion

claimBlocks.text: The NPS introduction identifies Arikara as a Caddoan language and describes farming villages and regional trade. It explicitly warns that expedition observers’ accounts were not necessarily correct from Indigenous perspectives and that the displayed excerpts have been adapted. These limits matter: similar-looking homes do not establish common origins, and an edited excerpt is distinct from an original journal.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Introductory editorial warning and contextual paragraphs, lines 24–29

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: A reconstruction used for public interpretation
claimBlocks.text: The NPS visitor entry identifies the Earthlodge Village near New Town as a reconstruction managed by MHA Nation. Its interpretation concerns Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara peoples together. The listing offers an introduction to public historical interpretation, rather than an unchanged ancestral settlement or an exclusively Arikara village; present visitor arrangements require separate checking.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Location and management fields; closing explanatory paragraph

inspections.method: Actual original homepage body read through mission, council, government and land sections; unrelated event/calendar listings not treated as historical research.
inspections.limits: No current population, acreage/land-title total, officeholder, job, contact, eligibility or service-access assertion adopted. Dynamic numbers display counter placeholders and underlying figures are not independently checked.

inspections.method: Two actual direct web opens timed out. Exact-original-URL web search then rendered the page’s extensive actual body, including substantive headings and paragraphs, not merely a search snippet or abstract. The named selected public historical sections were read there. Ordinary local HTTPS attempts to both known MHA pages failed with connection refusal and supplied no content.
inspections.limits: The page marks expanded tribal histories as work in progress. Its Arikara paragraph gives 1862 while the village timeline gives 1863; early 1860s avoids resolving that disagreement without further evidence. Old Mandan extinction/racial-purity judgments, sacred origins/bundles, detailed flag symbolism, demographic/casualty totals and present council rosters are excluded. MHA-wide dam impacts are not attributed exclusively to Arikara. Underlying treaties and archaeological studies not independently read.
inspections.inspectionAccess: Actual indexed original-page body; direct-fetch limit disclosed.

inspections.limits: Supporting only. No full journal collection, original manuscript, linked Ronda/Moulton book, private practice or underlying linguistic study inspected. Colonial prejudice and outsider judgments are not adopted; institutional hosted material is not automatically a faithful diplomatic transcription.

inspections.method: Actual short place-entry fields and explanatory paragraphs read; footer explicitly gives last updated June 1, 2021.
inspections.limits: An update date is not first publication or proof of present opening/services. Its illustration is specifically credited under CC BY-NC-ND 2.0, so no blanket NPS-media public-domain assumption is made; no image reused. A shared MHA visitor facility is not an exclusively Arikara historical site.

initialAdequacy.rationale: This pass refreshes six original access points and supplies a carefully scoped orientation from three substantive explanatory works, with three short supporting references. Initial adequacy is not yet established. Direct Sahnish-authored scholarship, actual language-learning publications, fuller historical primary records and contemporary Arikara-specific perspectives remain insufficient. An index or short contextual introduction cannot fill those gaps.
remainingLimits: The historical Nation page was inspected through its actual indexed body after direct timeouts; its selected interpretation and date disagreement require further corroboration.
The language portal explains educational priorities, but no linked textbook, handout, dictionary, class recording or language study was actually read.
The chapter and NPS introduction offer useful outside orientation, not a complete history or community review. The substantive target of twelve is not reached.

relationshipNote: Arikara/Sahnish is a distinct people within the shared Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation. Mandan and Hidatsa are allied constituent peoples, not aliases for Arikara. Fort Berthold is a reservation and governmental context, not the entirety of historical homelands. The three languages and Arikara-specific educational work require separate attention.
